_about: LanWatch port knowledge base. Key = port number (TCP unless 'protocol' says otherwise). risk: info | low | medium | high, judged for a device on a HOME network (ports found by LanWatch are reachable from the home network, not necessarily the internet). 'advice' lists article ids from remediation.json. Written by people, read by app/services/knowledge.py.

20.name: FTP data
20.what: Carries the files for an FTP file transfer.
20.why: Goes together with FTP on port 21, which sends passwords and files without encryption.

21.name: FTP (file transfer)
21.what: An old way to copy files to and from a device, often used by network storage (NAS), printers and cameras.
21.why: Passwords and files travel without encryption, so anyone on your network could read them.

22.name: SSH (secure remote login)
22.what: A secure way to log in to a device and control it by typing commands. Common on network storage, Raspberry Pi and Linux computers.
22.why: It is encrypted, so it is safe if the device has a strong password. A weak or default password is the main risk.

23.name: Telnet (old remote login)
23.what: An old way to log in to a device and control it by typing commands.
23.why: It sends everything, including passwords, without encryption. Anyone on your network could read them. Some cheap cameras and routers leave it on with a default password.

25.name: Email sending (SMTP)
25.what: Used to send email. Unusual on a home device unless it runs its own mail server.
25.why: Usually harmless at home, but unexpected on a device that shouldn't be sending email.

53.name: DNS (name look-ups)
53.what: Turns website names into addresses. Your router normally does this for every device at home.
53.why: Normal and expected on a router. On other devices it usually means an ad-blocker or home server is running.

80.name: Web page (HTTP)
80.what: A web page, very often a device's settings page (routers, printers, cameras, network storage).
80.why: Fine for most devices, but the page is not encrypted, so a password typed into it could be read by others on your network.

110.name: Email collection (POP3)
110.what: Used to collect email. Unusual on a home device.
110.why: Unencrypted; unexpected unless the device runs its own mail server.

111.name: RPC (Linux file sharing helper)
111.what: Helps other computers find file-sharing services on Linux machines and network storage.
111.why: Normal on network storage and Linux; not needed on most other devices.

135.name: Windows RPC
135.what: A Windows background service that lets Windows features talk to each other over the network.
135.why: Normal on Windows computers. Keep Windows updated.

137.name: NetBIOS name service
137.what: An old Windows way for computers to find each other by name.
137.why: Normal on Windows computers and network storage on a home network.

139.name: NetBIOS file sharing
139.what: Older Windows file and printer sharing.
139.why: Normal on Windows PCs and network storage, but it means files or printers may be shared with everyone on your network.

143.name: Email reading (IMAP)
143.what: Used to read email. Unusual on a home device.
143.why: Unencrypted; unexpected unless the device runs its own mail server.

161.name: SNMP (device monitoring)
161.what: Lets other devices read a device's status, often on printers and routers.
161.why: Old versions use a default password ('public') that lets anyone on your network read device details.

443.name: Secure web page (HTTPS)
443.what: An encrypted web page, often a device's settings page or app connection.
443.why: Encrypted, so this is the safe way for a settings page to work. Still use a strong admin password.

445.name: Windows file sharing (SMB)
445.what: Shares files and printers between computers. Used by Windows PCs and most network storage.
445.why: Normal on PCs and network storage. On other devices it is unexpected, and old versions of it have been a common way for malware to spread.

515.name: Printing (LPD)
515.what: An older way for computers to send print jobs.
515.why: Normal and expected on a network printer.

548.name: Apple file sharing (AFP)
548.what: Older Apple file sharing, used by Macs and some network storage.
548.why: Normal if you share files with Macs; otherwise it can be turned off.

554.name: Video stream (RTSP)
554.what: Live video from a camera, doorbell or baby monitor.
554.why: Some cameras allow anyone on the network to watch the stream, or use a default password.

631.name: Printing (IPP)
631.what: The modern way computers send print jobs to a printer.
631.why: Normal and expected on a network printer.

1883.name: MQTT (smart-home messages)
1883.what: Carries messages between smart-home devices (sensors, lights, Home Assistant).
1883.why: This port is unencrypted and is often set up without a password, so anyone on your network could read or send smart-home commands.

1900.name: UPnP (automatic port opening)
1900.what: Lets devices ask the router to open connections from the internet automatically, without asking you.
1900.why: Convenient for games and video calls, but a compromised device could use it to expose itself to the internet.

2049.name: NFS (Linux file sharing)
2049.what: Shares folders between Linux computers and network storage.
2049.why: Often set up without passwords, trusting every device on the network.

3000.name: Web app (port 3000)
3000.what: Often a home-server web app or a program's settings page.
3000.why: Usually fine if you know what it is; check it has a password.

3306.name: MySQL database
3306.why: Databases hold data directly and are often set up with weak passwords; it shouldn't be reachable by every device unless you need it.

3389.name: Remote Desktop (Windows)
3389.what: Lets someone see and control this Windows computer's screen from another device.
3389.why: Useful if you rely on it, but a common target for password guessing. Make sure it is meant to be on and the account has a strong password.

5000.name: UPnP / web app (port 5000)
5000.what: Often a router's UPnP service, a Synology NAS page, or an AirPlay receiver on Apple devices.
5000.why: Usually expected. On a router it often means UPnP is switched on.

5353.name: mDNS / Bonjour (device discovery)
5353.what: Lets devices find each other automatically (printers, AirPlay, Chromecast).

5432.name: PostgreSQL database
5432.why: Databases hold data directly; it shouldn't be reachable by every device unless you need it.

5900.name: VNC (remote screen control)
5900.what: Lets someone see and control this device's screen from another device.
5900.why: Many VNC set-ups use weak passwords or no encryption, giving full control of the device to anyone who gets in.

6379.name: Redis database
6379.what: A fast database often used by home-server apps.
6379.why: Redis often has no password by default, so anyone on your network could read or change its data.

7000.name: AirPlay
7000.what: Lets Apple devices stream music and video to this device.
7000.why: Normal on Apple TVs, Macs and AirPlay speakers.

8008.name: Chromecast / Google speaker
8008.what: Lets phones send video and music to a Chromecast or Google speaker.

8009.name: Chromecast / Google speaker (control)
8009.what: Controls a Google Cast device from a phone or computer.

8080.name: Web page (alternative port)
8080.what: A web page or settings page on a second port, common on cameras, routers and home servers.
8080.why: Like port 80: unencrypted, so check the device has a strong password.

8443.name: Secure web page (alternative port)
8443.what: An encrypted settings page on a second port.
8443.why: Encrypted, so generally fine. Use a strong admin password.

8883.name: MQTT over TLS (secure smart-home)
8883.why: The encrypted version of port 1883, so this is the safe way.

9100.name: Printing (raw / JetDirect)
9100.what: How computers send print jobs straight to a network printer.
9100.why: Normal and expected on a network printer.

27017.name: MongoDB database
27017.why: Older MongoDB set-ups have no password by default, so anyone on your network could read or change its data.

32400.name: Plex media server
32400.what: Streams your films, TV and music to other devices.
32400.why: Normal if you use Plex; keep it updated.

49152.name: UPnP / dynamic service
49152.what: Often a router's or smart TV's UPnP service, or another automatically chosen service.
49152.why: Usually expected. On a router it often means UPnP is switched on.

62078.name: Apple device sync
62078.what: Used by iPhones and iPads to sync with a computer over Wi-Fi.
62078.why: Normal on Apple phones and tablets.
